string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of the People’s Republic of China and one of its four direct-administered municipalities, which answer directly to the central government rather than to a province. More than 21 million people live there, and the city is the country’s political, cultural and diplomatic centre. Beijing has been a seat of power for most of the past eight centuries, and its heritage includes the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven, the Summer Palace and sections of the Great Wall, all recognised by UNESCO. It was the first city to host both the Summer Olympics (2008) and the Winter Olympics (2022).

Shanghai is one of China’s four direct-administered municipalities and one of the largest cities in the world, with close to 25 million residents. It lies on the Yangtze River estuary on the east coast and grew from a trading port opened to foreign commerce in the 1840s into a leading centre of finance, shipping and business. The Bund waterfront and the skyscrapers of Pudong’s Lujiazui district, including the Oriental Pearl Tower, are its best-known sights. The city is home to the Shanghai Stock Exchange, and its port is one of the busiest container ports in the world.

Chongqing, formerly romanized as Chungking, is a sprawling municipality in south-western China where the Jialing River meets the Yangtze. It was separated from Sichuan Province in 1997 to become the fourth and newest direct-administered municipality, covering about 82,400 square kilometres and home to over 30 million people, although much of that area is rural and mountainous. The steep hills of its urban core earned it the nickname “Mountain City”, and it is famous for spicy hotpot. During the Second Sino-Japanese War it served as the wartime capital of the Republic of China.

Tianjin is a direct-administered municipality on the Bohai Gulf in northern China, a short high-speed train ride from Beijing, with more than 13 million residents. Its name means “Heavenly Ford”, and the Haihe River winds through the city centre. Tianjin Port is one of the largest ports in northern China and a key gateway for trade. In the 19th century several foreign powers established concessions in the city, leaving streets of European-style buildings that now stand beside modern skyscrapers. Locals are also known for crosstalk comedy and snacks such as jianbing.
